title: Celebrating the future of computing on the Genesis Mission's first anniversary
content: Quantum Research Blog Celebrating the future of computing on the Genesis Mission's first anniversary One year after the launch of the Genesis Mission, IBM and its partners are advancing quantum-centric supercomputing for science, energy, and discovery. Date 24 Nov 2026 Authors Jerry Chow Topics Algorithms Systems Network Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key takeaways: The Genesis Mission aims to integrate quantum, AI, and high-performance computing to accelerate scientific discovery, energy innovation, and national security. IBM is contributing quantum hardware, software, and research to help advance quantum-centric supercomputing across government, industry, and academia. Recent initiatives span quantum error correction, quantum algorithms, fault-tolerant quantum computing, and applications in materials science, energy, and high-energy physics. IBM researchers are exploring hybrid quantum-classical approaches for materials simulation, molecular modeling, and fusion-energy research. IBM expects quantum, AI, and classical computing to work together as a unified compute framework for solving increasingly complex scientific challenges. One year ago, the US Department of Energy kicked off the Genesis Mission, a federal initiative launched to build an integrated quantum, AI, and high-performance computing platform for scientific discovery, energy innovation, and national security. To honor this anniversary, we are reprinting the below article, originally published in the Fall 2026 edition of Issues in Science and Technology . But things are moving fast. Even since publishing this story, IBM has made important progress toward realizing the mission’s objectives across quantum algorithms, scientific discovery, energy research, and the development of useful, fault-tolerant quantum systems. In the past month alone: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), IBM, and AMD launched a co-design platform for quantum error correction, combining IBM QPUs with AMD GPUs and CPUs to help researchers define and accelerate the classical and quantum workflows for scientifically relevant quantum computing applications in materials science, chemistry, and energy research. IBM deployed an IBM Quantum System Two with an IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processor at the University of Chicago's Hyde Park Labs to support the National Quantum Algorithm Center (NQAC) and the wider Illinois quantum ecosystem, advancing quantum algorithms and applications for use cases in drug discovery, energy, and high-energy physics. IBM and NVIDIA announced integration of the open-source Quantum Resource Management Interface (QRMI) with Slurm’s Hierarchical Resources (HRES) feature to give Slurm, the high-performance computing (HPC) workload manager NVIDIA develops, more visibility into quantum resources and workloads. IBM and NVIDIA, together with Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab), announced the upcoming launch of a modular quantum computing co-design platform to explore computationally demanding problems in high-energy and nuclear physics. IBM and AMD announced Pelagos , an open-source framework that tests quantum error correction decoders against billions of simulated error patterns on GPUs, helping accelerate the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing. As we celebrate the Genesis Mission’s first anniversary, we are excited to see the incredible progress toward building the future of computing as a community effort across government, industry, and academia, and even more excited about the path that lies ahead. The US Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission aspires to accelerate an evolution in computing that can help the United States address national and global challenges faster. The initiative connects the expertise and resources of DOE’s national laboratories with a consortium of the country’s leading industry, academic, and philanthropic organizations. As a Genesis consortium member, IBM is contributing access to its hardware, software, and research across artificial intelligence and quantum computing. More importantly, IBM’s involvement in Genesis provides its ecosystem of members and users across enterprises and universities with new opportunities to advance quantum-centric supercomputing. This combination of quantum, AI, and classical computing can soon be used to perform calculations beyond the ability of any single compute architecture, solving major hurdles in science that have previously strained classical-only systems. This capacity has been a long time in the making. Quantum computing emerged in the 1960s and ’70s from research studying the physics underlying computation itself. Both classical and quantum computers represent a unit of information as a string of binary digits.
